brut.title: London rents set to increase by 14 per cent over next five years | The Standard

webpage.text:
London rents set to increase by 14 per cent over next five years

Renters are not going to be given much relief any time soon, according to a new report. And while London rent might not climb so steeply as the rest of the country over the next five years, that’s simply because prices are already so high that tenants have hit an ‘affordability ceiling’ where they are already spending two fifths of their income on rent.

A new forecast by Savills says that UK rents will increase by 18 per cent over five years, including four per cent in 2025.

London rents will rise by 14.2 per cent by 2029 and increase by 2.5 per cent next year.

While tenant demand has come down from its record highs of 2021 and 2022, it remains at elevated levels, according to RICS. At the same time, the latest listings data indicates that the number of available rental listings per active letting branch was 16 per cent below their 2018-19 level in September.

As a result, properties are letting 20 per cent faster in 2024 than during 2018/19, and there is further upward pressure on prices.

Rental forecasts (source: Savills, Oxford Economic):

2024                   2025   2026    2027    2028    2029    2025-29
UK rental growth       4.0%   4.0%    3.5%    3.0%    3.0%    3.0%      17.6%
London rental growth   1.5%   2.5%    2.5%    2.5%    3.0%    3.0%      14.2%
UK income growth       2.9%   +2.9%   +2.6%   +2.5%   +3.1%   +3.0%     15.0%

“High demand and low supply have been the influence behind the significant rental growth seen over the past few years. At a national level, this pattern looks set to continue with rents expected to rise above incomes again,” says Guy Whittaker, research analyst at Savills.

“It is challenging to see where an increase in rental supply will come from in the next couple of years. The increase to the existing Stamp Duty Land Tax surcharge for second homes will likely dampen demand from new buy-to-let investors, and it will prevent some existing landlords from expanding their portfolios.

“The potential requirement to upgrade EPC [Energy Performance Certificate] ratings by 2030 may see some leave the sector altogether, particularly in markets where the upgrades required would exceed an entire year’s rental income. In those cases, it may make more financial sense to sell.”

Strong rental growth has stretched the finances of those living in the rental sector, limiting the capacity for further increases in some markets, specifically London: rental prices grew by four per cent nationally in the 12 months to September 2024, while London rents grew by just 1.5 per cent.

Nationally, Savills expects the imbalance of demand over supply will continue to override affordability in the short term, pushing up rents. Looking further ahead, Savills expects rental growth to be more aligned with income towards the end of the five-year period.

But in London, the market is already experiencing the drag effect of affordability. With Londoners spending as much as 43 per cent of their income in 2023, an inflection point appears to of been reached. It’s getting to a point where there is just no more money people can spend.

“Slower rental growth through 2023 has led to a slight easing of affordability pressures in London. We expect that this trend will continue in the near term with rental growth of 2.5 per cent in London in 2025, against income growth of 2.9 per cent,” Whittaker says.

“However, we expect to see more landlords exit the market, further eroding supply, and affordability will once again take a backseat. This would mean that rental growth could be stronger than we have currently forecast.”

brut.title: London West End property owner says business remains strong | Shaftesbury | The Guardian

webpage.text:
London West End property owner says business remains strong | Shaftesbury

Shaftesbury, the owner of property in London's Soho and other West End districts, says business has remained strong for its tenants despite some of the worst weather on record.

The company said demand has been strong across properties in Carnaby Street, Chinatown, Charlotte Street and other West End "villages" in the four months to 6 February. Existing sites were virtually fully let and businesses were snapping up refurbished properties as they came on the market.

At the end of December, properties making up 1.7% of Shaftesbury's estimated rental value were available to let, down from 2.3% at the end of September.

Shaftesbury bought up more sites in the final three months of 2013, acquiring shops, a restaurant, a bar and apartments in Charlotte Street and Chinatown. The company only owns property in the West End and focuses on upmarket or fashionable districts, including Covent Garden, once the location for the city's flower market but now booming with shops and bars.

A residential and shopping scheme on Carnaby Street, home to swinging London in the 1960s and now revamped as an upmarket shopping destination, has an estimated rental value of £2m compared with pre-development rental income of £1.6m.

The company said: "London's West End continues to be a popular destination for domestic and international visitors as well as Londoners. Despite exceptionally adverse weather conditions over the Christmas and New Year period, visitor numbers and spending, particularly in our restaurants, cafes and bars, have been resilient."

Shaftesbury's trading update is a further sign that London has emerged from the economic doldrums and is leading the UK's renewed economic growth. However, some economists have warned that the city is in the middle of a consumer bubble driven by rising property prices and household debt.

brut.title: We're sorry for letting thief into your home, says council | Society | The Guardian

webpage.text:
We're sorry for letting thief into your home, says council | Society

A council has been forced to apologise to one of its tenants after it helped a thief break in to a property.

While tenant James McLeod was away on holiday last year, Clackmannanshire council, based in Alloa, central Scotland, received a call from a man claiming that he had been locked out of his home.

The council sent one of its maintenance staff to help Richard Strachan force the door of the flat in Sauchie, near Alloa.

The council's repairman also changed the locks on the property and issued Strachan with a set of keys. He then stole hundreds of pounds worth of possessions from the home.

Strachan admitted four charges of housebreaking and was given 300 hours community service, the Daily Telegraph reported.

Clackmannanshire council apologised to Mr McLeod. Its head of property services, Gordon Stewart, said: "On behalf of the council, my apologies go to the tenant concerned in this housebreaking."

But he insisted: "This was an isolated incident and I can reassure tenants that our policy and practices have now been tightened to ensure that incidents like this cannot be repeated."

brut.title: More affordable housing promised in White Paper - BBC News

webpage.text:
More affordable housing promised in White Paper

The government has vowed to build more affordable houses and help people buy and rent, after admitting the current market is "broken".

The new housing strategy for England includes giving councils powers to pressurise developers to start building on land they own.

Ministers also pledged to make renting more "family-friendly" with longer tenancies offered.

Labour called the measures announced "feeble beyond belief".

 * Rolling updates: Brexit, Speaker row and Housing

 * Housing crisis: Why not use empty homes?

 * Mark Easton: How radical are the plans?

 * House price growth 'to slow in 2017'

 * Will it get easier to build on the green belt?

The government says at least 250,000 new homes are needed each year to keep pace with demand and councils and developers need to "get real" to the scale of the challenge.

Mr Javid set out the details of the housing White Paper, external in a statement to MPs, with measures including:

 * Forcing councils to produce an up-to-date plan for housing demand

 * Expecting developers to avoid "low-density" housing where land availability is short

 * Encouraging the extension of buildings upwards in urban areas

 * Reducing the time allowed between planning permission and the start of building from three to two years

 * Using a £3bn fund to help smaller building firms challenge major developers, including support for off-site construction, where parts of buildings are assembled in a factory

 * A "lifetime ISA" to help first-time buyers save for a deposit

 * Maintaining protection for the green belt, which can only be built on "in exceptional circumstances"

 * Introducing banning orders "to remove the worst landlords or agents from operating"

 * Banning letting agents' fees

So-called starter homes, championed by former Prime Minister David Cameron, will be aimed at "households that need them most", those with combined incomes of less than £80,000, or £90,000 in London.

Starter homes are new homes built for first-time buyers between 23 and 40 years old and sold at least 20% below market value. The maximum price after the discount has been applied is £250,000 outside London and £450,000 in the capital.

Under the new proposals, starter home buyers will need a mortgage, "to stop cash buyers", and some or all of the discount will have to be repaid if the property is resold within 15 years, "to reduce the risk of speculation".

A proposal that 20% of all larger developments had to be starter homes is to be dropped and replaced with a "clear expectation" that at least 10% of developments will be "affordable home ownership units".

The Local Government Association said the White Paper contained "some encouraging signs" on increasing housing supply and affordability.

It welcomed the new "flexibility" around starter homes and called for new power and funding to allow councils to build affordable homes directly.

The Campaign to Protect Rural England welcomed what it said was a focus on addressing current failings rather than "meddling" with the planning system.

"We are pleased that ministers have recognised that weakening the Green Belt is unnecessary," said chief executive Shaun Spiers. "But with 360,000 houses already proposed for Green Belt land the government needs to do much more to uphold national policy and stop councils releasing it for development."

Daniel Bentley, editorial director at the think tank Civitas, said: "The problem is not sites with planning permission standing idle, except in limited circumstances.

"It is with sites that are being developed, but too slowly to get ahead of demand and make any difference to the affordability of housing."

Graeme Brown, interim chief executive of the homelessness charity Shelter, said: "The White Paper poses the right questions. What we need now is quick and bold action that helps people in need of a decent home tomorrow, not in 10 years."

 4.  Facebook to fact-check photos and videospublished at 09:51 BST 14 September 2018
     09:51 BST 14 September 2018
     
     Facebook is introducing a new tool that will help the company to fact-check photos and videos.
     
     It's part of the firm's latest efforts to stop fake news and misinformation from spreading on its site.
     
     Once the system identifies an image or video that it suspects was altered, human fact checkers then try to verify if the content is real or not.
     
     Until now, most of Facebook's fact-checkers have focused on reviewing articles and posts.
     
     The sharing of visual content "creates an easy opportunity for manipulation by bad actors" who make it appear that someone did or said something they did not, the company said in a statement., external
     
     The measures come as Facebook ramps up its fact-checking efforts to protect future elections from foreign interference.

 5.  Voodoo bosspublished at 09:35 BST 14 September 2018
     09:35 BST 14 September 2018
     
     The annual Ig Nobel Prize - "for achievements that first make people laugh then make them think" - has a category for economics and this year's winner is a corker.
     
     A group of academics, external won for "investigating whether it is effective for employees to use Voodoo dolls to retaliate against abusive bosses".
     
     People were asked to think about a time their boss had abused or bullied them - 50% were then given a chance to unleash their anger on a virtual voodoo doll.
     
     Douglas Brown, who was a member of the team, told The Guardian: "Relative to those who did not stab and torture a voodoo doll, those who stabbed the doll representing their boss felt a greater sense of fairness and justice.”
     
     While he suggested people may want to find other ways to express their frustration: "I personally don’t see any harm in torturing a voodoo doll, if it makes you feel better.”

 6.  Carney's train of thoughtpublished at 09:23 BST 14 September 2018
     09:23 BST 14 September 2018
     
     Today Programme
     BBC Radio 4
     
     BBC economics editor Kamal Ahmed explains the reasoning behind the Bank of England's thinking about what could happen in the event of a no-deal Brexit.
     
     He says that if the pound falls in this doomsday scenario, inflation builds which makes food and fuel imports more expensive.
     
     "In that situation, the Bank then raises interest rates to try and control inflation and also to support the economy because raising interest rates takes money out of the economy and stops the velocity of inflation," he says.
     
     "Of course that means that people's mortgages become more expensive. If your mortgages are more expensive it means less people are likely to buy if there is consumer stress already and economic stress already the housing market is affected."
     
     He adds: "I don't believe the Governor believes this is what will happen in a no-deal scenario. It is that they have 'over-tested' the banks to ensure that there would not be any type of calamity even if there is a no deal."

liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: British Steel has announced that it will cut 400 managerial, professional and administrative roles across its UK, Ireland, France and the Netherlands operations "as part of the company’s ongoing transformation."

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Oil prices volatile after Thursday's fall
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody:
Oil prices have bounced around so far today, after sharp falls on Thursday. Brent is up 5 cents at $78.23 a barrel, West Texas Intermediate is up by 22 cents at $68.81. ANZ Research said: "Prices remain well supported as the market continues to
fret about ongoing structural supply issues elsewhere." On Thursday, the Paris-based International Energy Agency, said it expects world
oil demand would reach 100 million barrels per day (bpd) in the next three months. But it said: "As we move into 2019, a possible risk to our forecast lies
in some key emerging economies, partly due to currency
depreciations versus the US dollar, raising the cost of
imported energy. "In addition, there is a risk to growth from an escalation
of trade disputes."

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Facebook to fact-check photos and videos
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Facebook is introducing a new tool that will help the company to fact-check photos and videos. It's part of the firm's latest efforts to stop fake news and misinformation from spreading on its site. Once the system identifies an image or video that it suspects was altered, human fact checkers then try to verify if the content is real or not. Until now, most of Facebook's fact-checkers have focused on reviewing articles and posts. The sharing of visual content "creates an easy opportunity for manipulation by bad actors" who make it appear that someone did or said something they did not, the company said in a statement. The measures come as Facebook ramps up its fact-checking efforts to protect future elections from foreign interference.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Voodoo boss
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: The annual Ig Nobel Prize - "for achievements that first make people laugh then make them think" - has a category for economics and this year's winner is a corker. A group of academics won for "investigating whether it is effective for employees to use Voodoo dolls to retaliate against abusive bosses". People were asked to think about a time their boss had abused or bullied them - 50% were then given a chance to unleash their anger on a virtual voodoo doll. Douglas Brown, who was a member of the team, told The Guardian: "Relative to those who did not stab and torture a voodoo doll, those who stabbed the doll representing their boss felt a greater sense of fairness and justice.”  While he suggested people may want to find other ways to express their frustration: "I personally don’t see any harm in torturing a voodoo doll, if it makes you feel better.”

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Carney's train of thought
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: BBC economics editor Kamal Ahmed explains the reasoning behind the Bank of England's thinking about what could happen in the event of a no-deal Brexit. He says that if the pound falls in this doomsday scenario, inflation builds which makes food and fuel imports more expensive. "In that situation, the Bank then raises interest rates to try and control inflation and also to support the economy because raising interest rates takes money out of the economy and stops the velocity of inflation," he says. "Of course that means that people's mortgages become more expensive. If your mortgages are more expensive it means less people are likely to buy if there is consumer stress already and economic stress already the housing market is affected." He adds: "I don't believe the Governor believes this is what will happen in a no-deal scenario. It is that they have 'over-tested' the banks to ensure that there would not be any type of calamity even if there is a no deal."

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Weak dollar makes pound look good
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody:
The pound has perked up a little this morning. It's currently trading at $1.3134, up almost a third of a cent. Analysts say the move reflects weakness in the dollar, rather than any strength in the pound. "The bigger move is the US dollar. It's a continuation of
yesterday after weaker U.S. inflation data," said Esther
Reichelt, an analyst at Commerzbank.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Asian stocks mostly higher on trade talk hopes
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Asian stocks were broadly higher on hopes that US and China could resume trade talks as fresh US tariffs loom. The rise came even as US President Donald Trump poured cold water on the prospects of a US-China trade deal. He said the pressure was on China, not on the US, to achieve a deal. Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 rose 1.2% to 23,094.67, while South Korea's benchmark Kospi index was up 1.4%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 index added 0.6% In China, Hong Kong's Hang Seng index rose 0.99% but the Shanghai Composite slipped 0.2%. A key gauge of infrastructure spending fell to a record low.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Bank always examines doomsday scenarios
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: House prices could fall by 35% over the next three years if there is a no-deal Brexit, according to a briefing Bank of England Governor Mark Carney gave to MPs. However, BBC economics editor Kamal Ahmed says it is important to remember that this is not a forecast by the Bank of England but an examination of the worst-case scenarios. He tells the Today programme: "The Bank goes through this process, as it has done since the financial crisis, of doomsday scenarios that it builds [to test the banking system]. "It doesn't mean that it reasonably expects this to happen if there is a no deal scenario."

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Investec shares soar on spin-off
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Investec shares have jumped 12%. The company, which sponsors club rugby in the southern hemisphere, has announced plans to hive off and list its asset management unit. The Anglo-South African investment bank said "it is now appropriate to demerge and publicly list" the business. Investec's remaining company will be made up of its specialist banking and wealth & investment businesses.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Food boosts Co-op Group sales
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Co-op said that like-for-like food sales grew by 4.4% in the six months to 7 July.  Food and the acquisition of convenience store chain Nisa Retail Limited in May drove total revenue up 10% to £5bn while pre-tax profit grew to £26m from £14m last year. Chairman Allan Leighton said: "Against a backdrop of increasing national uncertainty, I'm pleased that the Co-op has continued to perform successfully during the first half of the year."

liveBlogUpdate.headline: ITV could get Britbox boost
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Shares in ITV have risen 1% this morning. Analysts at Liberum have made positive comments about ITV. They estimate that ITV's share of Britbox, a venture with the BBC and AMC, could be worth £500m. Britbox generates "tens of millions of dollars in sales" and Liberum says it is likely to grow as it is launched in other countries.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: FTSE 100 opens higher
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: The FTSE 100 has made healthy gains in the early going.  The index is up 27 points at 7,308. That's more or less what it lost on Thursday.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: VW Beetle comes to the end of the road
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Volkswagen is ending production of its Beetle in 2019, closing the door on one of the world's most iconic car designs. The German company said output would end at its plant in Mexico next July after production of celebration models. The Beetle has its roots in Nazi Germany with the creation of a "people's car", but went on to star in a series of successful Disney films as a vehicle called Herbie. But sales, particularly in the key US market, have fallen in recent years. Read more here.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: ANZ under fire over 2015 share placement
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Australia's corporate regulator has started legal proceedings against ANZ over a share placement in 2015. The Australian Securities & Investments Commission says ANZ failed "to notify the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) that approximately A$791 million of the A$2.5 billion ($1.8bn, £1.4bn) of ANZ shares offered in the Placement was to be acquired by its underwriters rather than placed with investors," it says in a media release. Australia's consumer watchdog said in June ANZ, Deutsche Bank and Citigroup would be prosecuted on criminal cartel charges. The allegations concerned arrangements for the sale of A$2.5bn worth of ANZ shares in 2015.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Tim Martin wants 'considerable immigration'
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Brexit supporter and JD Wetherspoon founder Tim Martin said the UK will need "a considerable level of immigration" over the next three decades "to be a successful economy". However, he also tells the Today Programme: "Uncontrolled immigration, EU style, is not a good thing and it has probably kept people's wages down a bit".

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Wetherspoon pubs not planning cutbacks
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: The pub chain JD Wetherspoon has warned that it expects prices to rise over the next year. So will it cut costs and staff? Probably not, according to Tim Martin, the founder of JD Wetherspoon. He told the Today Programme that companies on the stock exchange "try too hard" to cut their costs and end up reducing customers service. "I think what we'll do is keep our prices as low we reasonably can, they might have to go up a little bit, and just do the right thing and hope that is compensated by rising sales which will pay for the cost increases," he said.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Clouds ahead for RBS and Ross McEwan
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: In a week that marks the 10-year anniversary of the start of the global financial crisis, RBS's chief executive Ross McEwan has been accused by MPs of withholding information about an investigation into criminal activity within the bank. Maike Currie, investment director at Fidelity International, says this is serious: "Because he is being accused of withholding information, misleading parliament and at a time when we are seeing the 10 year anniversary of the financial crisis where people are asking questions about whether the culture of banks has fundamentally changed. "This doesn't bode well for the bank or for Ross McEwan."

liveBlogUpdate.headline: Church should keep Amazon stock
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: The Archbishop of Canterbury ruffled feathers when he accused online shopping giant Amazon of "leeching off the taxpayer" - especially as it emerged that the Church of England is a shareholder in the company and doesn't intend to sell its shares. Maike Currie, investment director at Fidelity International, says that Church of England is right to keep its stock. "Engagement is key," she says. "You can only drive change from within so engagement is becoming more and more important, it is high on the agenda of investment companies. I do think you achieve more by being in the room."

liveBlogUpdate.headline: JD Wetherspoon warns of rising costs
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Pub chain JD Wetherspoon says it has had a "reasonable" start to its financial year.  It has a rather unusual financial year, the most recent one ended on 29 July. During that year it made pre-tax profits of £89m, up 16.5% on the previous year. Like-for-like sales were up 5%. However, founder Tim Martin expects rising taxes, labour and interest costs in the current financial year.
